title: Azure service credential exposed by a reporting vendor at a regional lender
summary: A stranger's email warning that one of the company's Azure credentials is public sits unread in a shared mailbox for two days. The credential belongs to a reporting vendor and can read a storage account holding 14 months of borrower exports, and the Azure invoice shows a surge in outbound data nobody can explain. The exercise tests whether the company can cut off a vendor quickly, decide without storage logs, and meet the regulator's 72-hour notice and the card processor's contract clause.

setting.company_profile: A 120-person regional consumer lender with an on-premises file server and Active Directory, Microsoft 365, reporting workloads in Azure and a loan servicing system hosted by its vendor. It is supervised by a state financial regulator, and card payments are handled by an outside processor.
setting.day_and_time: Thursday, 3:40 p.m., the day before the month-end report is due to the funding bank
setting.initial_signal: The receptionist, clearing the shared info@ mailbox, forwards an email to the IT lead. It was sent two days ago by someone who says they are a security researcher, and it claims a working credential for the company's Azure environment is visible in a public code repository. That morning accounts payable had asked why the latest Azure invoice shows outbound data charges 14 times higher than normal.

roles.name: Incident Commander
roles.responsibilities: Takes charge once the stranger's report is checked, decides when the reporting vendor's access is cut off, and keeps the regulator and processor deadlines in front of the group.

roles.name: Technical Lead
roles.responsibilities: Disables the exposed credential in Microsoft Entra ID, reviews the vendor's other access through Azure, the VPN and Active Directory, and reports what the sign-in logs and the invoice can and cannot show.

roles.name: Communications Lead
roles.responsibilities: Prepares what borrowers, customer service staff and the funding bank are told, and handles the reply to the person who reported the exposure.

roles.name: Legal and Compliance Lead
roles.responsibilities: Settles with outside counsel when the company determined that an incident occurred, files the notice with the state financial regulator, and reads the vendor and processor contracts.

roles.name: Executive Sponsor
roles.responsibilities: Approves cutting off the reporting vendor before the month-end report, signs off the regulator notice and briefs the board chair.

roles.name: Scribe
roles.responsibilities: Records every finding, decision and time, above all when the report was received, read and confirmed, because the regulator will ask.

objectives: Show that a security report from an outsider reaches someone who can act on it within one business day, whichever mailbox it lands in.
Decide who has authority to disable a vendor's credential when doing so stops a report the business needs.
Decide what counts as the moment the company determined an incident occurred, and who files the 72-hour notice with the regulator.
Confirm the team can list every way a vendor gets in: Azure, the VPN, Active Directory and the loan servicing system.
Decide whether borrower data is treated as taken when storage logging was never switched on, and who makes that call.

injects.title: A stranger's warning, two days old
injects.narrative: Thursday, 3:40 p.m. The receptionist, clearing the shared info@ mailbox, forwards an email to the IT lead. It was sent on Tuesday at 9:12 a.m. by someone who says they are a security researcher. It claims that a working credential for the company's Azure environment is visible in a public code repository belonging to another organization, gives a link and asks for a security contact. It does not ask for money. The IT lead cannot tell whether it is genuine or bait to get someone to click. Separately, accounts payable asked this morning why the latest Azure invoice shows outbound data charges 14 times higher than normal. The email went to info@ because the company's website lists no contact for reporting security problems.
questions: Who decides whether this email is a real report or a scam, and how is the link checked without putting a work computer at risk?
Taken together, do the email and the invoice make this an incident now, and who declares it?
Who replies to the sender, and what may and may not be said?
expected_actions: The IT lead opens the link on a computer kept off the company network and checks whether the application ID it shows matches an app registered in Microsoft Entra ID, the sign-in directory behind Microsoft 365 and Azure, without trying the credential.
Declare a suspected incident, name the Incident Commander, and have the Scribe log three times: email received, email read, incident declared.
Send the reporter a short acknowledgment from a monitored mailbox with a named contact and no detail about the company's systems.

injects.title: The credential belongs to the reporting vendor, and the vendor is in no hurry
injects.narrative: The report is genuine. The repository belongs to a developer at the company's reporting vendor, the analytics firm behind the monthly portfolio reports. One file holds the service credential, a sign-in used by software rather than a person, that the vendor's nightly job uses to read loan data exports in an Azure storage account. It has been public for 11 days. Reached at 4:30 p.m., the vendor's account manager says the developer has gone home and proposes replacing the credential at Tuesday's maintenance window. The IT lead could disable it in Microsoft Entra ID in two minutes, but the nightly job would stop, and the month-end report is due at 5:00 p.m. tomorrow to the bank that funds the company's loans. The vendor also has a VPN account and an Active Directory account for the on-premises file server.
questions: Who has the authority to disable a vendor's credential today, knowing the month-end report may be late, and does the plan say so?
Does the company also disable the vendor's VPN and Active Directory accounts until it knows what else was in that repository, and who decides?
Who tells the funding bank that the report may be late, and when?
expected_actions: Disable the service credential in Microsoft Entra ID now, without waiting for the vendor's maintenance window, and record the time.
Disable the vendor's VPN account and its Active Directory account until the vendor confirms in writing what else the repository contained.
Require the vendor, in writing, to take the repository out of public view today, keep a copy for the investigation and name a senior contact for tonight.

injects.title: Fourteen months of borrower records and no record of who read them
injects.narrative: By 6:00 p.m. the IT lead has looked inside the storage account. Every night the loan servicing system, hosted by its own vendor, exports borrower records there. Nobody set a rule to delete old files, so 14 months of exports are sitting in it: names, addresses, Social Security numbers, loan balances and the bank details used for automatic payments, for about 61,000 borrowers. The exposed credential could read all of it. The Microsoft Entra ID sign-in log shows the credential used from two locations that are not the reporting vendor's offices on nine of the last 11 days. But the storage account's own logging, which would show which files were read, was never switched on. The reporting vendor says the surge in outbound data on the invoice was its own job reloading the full history last week.
questions: The sign-in log and the vendor's explanation point in different directions: does the company treat the records of 61,000 borrowers as taken, and who decides?
What does the company need from the vendor to test its explanation, and who demands it tonight?
Who can approve hiring outside forensic investigators this evening to examine the logs, and who picks them?
expected_actions: Export the Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs and the Azure activity log for the credential before they expire, and store copies where the vendor has no access.
Ask the reporting vendor in writing for its job run history and the network addresses its systems use, with a deadline of 9:00 a.m. tomorrow.
Treat the borrower exports as copied until evidence shows otherwise, write that decision in the log, and switch on logging for the storage account so access from now on is recorded.

injects.title: The 72-hour question: when did the company know?
injects.narrative: At 7:15 p.m. the compliance officer joins the call. The state financial regulator requires notice within 72 hours of the company determining that a cybersecurity incident has occurred. The stranger's email arrived at 9:12 a.m. on Tuesday, 58 hours ago, but nobody with authority read it until this afternoon. Outside counsel, reached at home, says the clock runs from the determination, not from the moment an email landed in a mailbox, but that the regulator will ask why a warning sat unread for two days and exactly when the determination was made. The chief executive does not want to file anything until it is certain that data was taken, and would rather wait for the vendor's findings. The compliance officer says an early notice can be updated later; a late one cannot be undone.
questions: At what moment did the company determine that an incident occurred, who made that determination, and is the time written down?
Who decides between filing now with incomplete facts and waiting for the vendor, and who settles a disagreement between the chief executive and the compliance officer?
Who drafts the notice, who reviews it and who submits it to the regulator?
expected_actions: The Legal and Compliance Lead agrees the determination time with outside counsel, records it and sets the filing deadline 72 hours from it with a named owner.
Draft the regulator notice tonight from confirmed facts only: what was exposed, since when, what has been disabled and what is still unknown.
The Executive Sponsor briefs the board chair by phone, and the Scribe logs who approved the decision to file.

injects.title: Card details that were not supposed to be there
injects.narrative: Friday, 8:30 a.m. The compliance officer has been telling everyone that no card data is involved, because card payments are handled entirely by the outside processor. The reporting analyst opens one export file to check and finds columns added in March for borrowers who pay by debit card: card type, last four digits and expiry date. Full card numbers are not there. The processor agreement requires the company to tell the processor within 24 hours of any suspected compromise of card data, and nobody in the room is sure whether these fields count. One manager argues that calling will trigger an expensive review for nothing. Meanwhile the reporting vendor has sent its job history. It accounts for about a third of the outbound data on the invoice. The rest is unexplained.
questions: Who decides whether the processor is told today, and should the company ask the processor whether these fields count instead of deciding alone?
Who should have to approve a change to what leaves the loan servicing system, such as the card fields added in March?
With two thirds of the outbound data unexplained, who updates the regulator and by when?
expected_actions: The Legal and Compliance Lead phones the processor's risk contact this morning, describes the fields involved and asks for the processor's position in writing.
The reporting analyst lists every field in the export files so that each notice describes the data accurately.
Put the regulator, the processor, the funding bank and borrower notices on one tracker with deadline, owner and status.

injects.title: The report is due, the vendor wants back in and borrowers have not been told
injects.narrative: Friday, 1:00 p.m. The month-end report is due to the funding bank at 5:00 p.m., and the nightly job has been off since the exposed credential was shut down. The reporting vendor asks for a new credential with the same rights as the old one so it can finish the report this afternoon. Its chief executive also emails: the vendor's own review found no evidence of misuse, and it asks not to be named in any notice. The loan servicing system's vendor confirms the exports contain the fields the analyst listed. Customer service supervisors want to know what to say if borrowers call. The company's chief executive wants three decisions from the group by 2:00 p.m.: how the report gets done, whether the vendor is let back in, and when borrowers are told.
questions: Does the reporting vendor get a new credential today, with what limits, and who approves it?
How does the month-end report get finished by 5:00 p.m., or who tells the funding bank it will be late?
Who decides when borrowers are told and whether the vendor is named, given the vendor's request?
expected_actions: If access is restored, the Technical Lead issues a new credential limited to the current month's export folder, set to expire in 30 days, with storage logging on.
The Executive Sponsor phones the funding bank before 5:00 p.m. with a new delivery time and a plain account of why.
Give customer service a short approved script and one escalation contact, and agree a date for borrower notice letters with outside counsel.

wrap_up_questions: Where did the plan tell the group who decides, and where did people argue about authority instead?
What was missing: a monitored address for security reports, a list of every vendor's access, logging on storage that holds borrower data, or a written rule for when the 72-hour clock starts?
Which changes to the plan, the vendor contracts and the Azure setup come out of this exercise, and when is each due?
Who is named as owner for each change, and how does the compliance officer show the board it was made?
